turns.content: ok so i need a reality check. am i being super petty and territorial here or is it genuinely messed up that aris gave mateo the principal director slot on a project i literally wrote the grant for on my own time? like i keep going back and forth between being furious and thinking maybe i'm just being a dramatic non-phd who doesn't know how academia works 💀

Not petty. Also not necessarily a conspiracy. Both things can be true, so let me split it up.

**The part that's legitimately annoying, full stop:** you did the intellectual heavy lifting, unpaid, and someone else's name is going on the front of it. That stings no matter what the org chart says, and being mad about it doesn't make you dramatic. It makes you a person who did the work.

**The part where academia is genuinely weird:** "who wrote the grant" and "who is PI/principal director" are often just... different questions there. A lot of funders and institutions require the PI to have a PhD, a faculty appointment, or a specific title, sometimes for boring compliance reasons (who's legally accountable for the money, who can sign off on IRB stuff, etc.). If that's what's going on, Aris may have had less choice than it looks like. Doesn't make it fair, but it makes it structural rather than personal.

**The actual test of whether it's messed up** is less about the slot and more about the handling:

- Did Aris *talk to you* before deciding, or did you find out after?
- Are you listed as co-I / co-PI / anything visible, or are you invisible on the thing you built?
- Did anyone explain *why*? "Funder requires it" is a real reason. Silence or "that's just how it works" is not.
- Is there anything in it for you—authorship, title bump, money, a stated role in leading the work day-to-day?

If the answer to most of those is "no, no one told me anything, and I'm just in the acknowledgments," then yeah, that's a real grievance and you should raise it. If it was a structural constraint but nobody bothered to loop you in or credit you properly, that's still a legit complaint, just a different one ("I get *why*, but the way it was done sucked").

So which was it—did you get a heads up and a reason, or did you find out from the paperwork?

i think i need to show you the email aris sent with the draft credit blurbs. bc seeing it in writing hit different. he has mateo down as "conceptual vision" for the whole program. i'm listed under "operations support." 💀 does that count as theft or am i overreacting

Okay, "conceptual vision" vs. "operations support" is not a compliance technicality. That's a narrative about who thought and who typed. If you wrote the grant, the concept *is* the thing you did.

I haven't actually seen the email yet, so paste it in or attach it and I'll read the exact wording. But going off your description:

**"Theft" is probably the wrong word, and I'd avoid it out loud** because it puts Aris on the defensive and makes it easy to dismiss you as emotional. **"Misattribution" is the right word**, and it's a real, nameable problem in academia that people take seriously. Credit blurbs are how a project gets remembered. If this goes out as written, five years from now the story is "Mateo's program, with some help."

**You're not overreacting.** The fact that it's a *draft* is actually the good news. Drafts exist to be corrected, and Aris sending it around is an implicit invitation to weigh in. This is the moment.

Rough shape of the response I'd send: calm, factual, specific.

- "Thanks for circulating these. I want to flag that 'operations support' doesn't reflect my role. I wrote the grant proposal, including the [aims / framing / program design], on my own time."
- Propose the fix: "Something like 'program design and grant development' (or co-conceptualization) would be accurate."
- Optionally attach or reference the drafts with timestamps. Not as a threat, just as receipts.

That's it. No "I feel disrespected," no history of grievances. Just "this is inaccurate, here's the correction."

Send me the email and I'll help you tune the wording to how Aris actually writes. Also tell me: is there any chance Mateo genuinely contributed to the concept, or was he not in the room at all?

ok here's the email. he cc'd the whole project team which is honestly the worst part 💀

"Dear team, please review draft credit blurbs for the Starlit Horizons launch roster. Principal Director/Conceptual Vision: Dr. Mateo Vance. Operations and Logistics Lead: Suki Chen. Beta-test coordination: [etc]."

that's it. no explanation. no "hey suki i know you did the actual work but here's why." just... that.

Okay, now that I've seen it: this is not you being a dramatic non-PhD. This is a bad email.

Not evil-bad. Lazy-bad. Which in some ways is worse, because there's no story to argue with. Aris didn't build a case for why Mateo is "Conceptual Vision." He just... typed it, hit send to everyone, and moved on. That reads less like a deliberate snub and more like he genuinely doesn't have the picture of who did what. Or has it and didn't think it through. Either way, the effect is the same: a whole team just watched your work get filed under "logistics."

A couple of things I'd pull out of the actual text:

- **"Operations and Logistics Lead" is not nothing.** It's a real title with "Lead" in it. But it's the wrong title. It describes coordinating a thing, not conceiving it. If you wrote the grant, the concept is yours, and the blurb is factually inaccurate.
- **"Dr." on Mateo, no honorific on you.** Small, but it quietly does the "who's the thinker here" work. Worth noticing, not worth fighting about.
- **The cc is the worst part, and also your leverage.** He made it public. That means the correction can also be public, and it'll look completely normal because he literally asked for review.

Here's the move. Reply-all (yes, all; he set that norm), short, zero heat:

> Hi Aris, thanks for circulating. One correction on my line: I developed the Starlit Horizons concept and wrote the grant proposal, so "Operations and Logistics Lead" understates the role. Suggest "Program Design & Grant Development Lead" (or "Co-Conceptual Lead"), with operations listed as well if useful. Happy to talk through it if helpful. — Suki

That's the whole thing. It's a factual edit to a draft, delivered in the same register he used. It doesn't accuse anyone, doesn't mention Mateo, and puts your claim on the record in front of the same people who saw the original. If Aris wants to keep "Conceptual Vision" on Mateo after that, he now has to explain *why*, in writing, to the team. That's a much harder position than the one he's in right now.

Then, separately and privately, I'd ask Aris for ten minutes. Not to relitigate the email. To ask the question that actually matters: "Going forward, how are you thinking about my role in this? I want to make sure the grant work translates into something real." That conversation is where you find out if this was carelessness or a pattern.

Do you have the grant drafts with dates somewhere you can lay hands on quickly? You probably won't need them, but knowing they exist will make you a lot calmer hitting send.

lmao ok you're right the reply-all is the power move actually. 💀 i just stare at the "conceptual vision" line and feel my soul leave my body. but if i reply-all with just the facts, it puts the ball in his court in front of everyone. do i send it now or wait until his office hours monday?

Write it now. Send it Monday morning. Do not wait for office hours to send it.

Reasoning on each piece:

**Write it now** because you're clear-headed enough to be strategic and annoyed enough to be motivated. That's the ideal drafting state. Get it out of your head and into a draft so you stop staring at "conceptual vision" and feeling your soul detach.

**Don't send it at 6:35 on a Saturday.** A reply-all at dawn on a weekend reads as "I have been awake all night about this," which is exactly the emotional-not-factual vibe you want to avoid. The words can be perfectly calm and the timestamp will still narrate for you. Schedule it (or just sit on it) for Monday around 8–9am so it lands at the top of everyone's inbox as a normal, boring, businesslike correction to a draft. Which is what it is.

**Don't wait for office hours, though.** If you bring it up privately first, the correction happens in a room with two people and the team never sees it. Then it's Aris's version of the conversation that gets relayed, if it gets relayed at all. The email needs to exist on the record *before* you sit down with him. Then office hours becomes the follow-up: "You saw my note on the blurbs. I wanted to talk about how you're thinking about my role going forward." Much stronger footing than opening cold with "so about that email."

One caveat: did he give a deadline for feedback on the roster? If there's any chance it gets finalized over the weekend or first thing Monday, send Sunday evening instead. Otherwise, Monday morning.

And yeah, dig up those dated grant drafts this weekend. You won't attach them. You'll just know they're there.

ok i drafted it. "hi aris, correction on my credit line. i originated the starlit horizons concept and wrote the pilot grant. suggest 'program design and grant development lead' instead of ops support. happy to discuss." good? or too stiff?

Not too stiff. Stiff is the goal here. It's a factual edit to a draft, and you nailed the register. Three small tweaks:

1. **Quote his actual wording.** He wrote "Operations and Logistics Lead," not "ops support." Using his exact phrase makes it read as a precise correction rather than a paraphrase with feelings in it.
2. **One softener at the top.** "Correction on my credit line" as an opener lands a little like a slap. "Thanks for circulating" costs you nothing and buys you the tone.
3. **Match his capitalization.** He wrote "Dear team" with proper caps. Lowercase-casual next to that reads slightly off in a reply-all.

Cleaned up:

> Hi Aris, thanks for circulating these. One correction on my line: I originated the Starlit Horizons concept and wrote the pilot grant, so "Operations and Logistics Lead" doesn't quite capture the role. Suggest "Program Design and Grant Development Lead" instead. Happy to discuss.
>
> Suki

Same content as yours, just tightened. Schedule it for Monday morning, close the tab, and go do literally anything else this weekend.
